system: 9n+1 (even n -> n/2, odd n -> 9n+1), GLOBAL: is every orbit eventually periodic?
best_route: The expected answer is 'no'. There are two ways to get it. (i) Show that 9n+1 has no cycles at all, which settles it immediately because a non-eventually-periodic orbit is unbounded. (ii) Show that one specific orbit diverges. Route (i) is the more structured one: the cycle equation n(2^K - 9^k) = sum 9^{k-1-i} 2^{A_i}, Baker/Rhin bounds on |K log2 - 2k log3|, then the Simons-de Weger m-cycle machinery. The missing lemma is a bound on cycles that does not depend on the number m of local minima. That is the same lemma whose absence keeps 'Collatz has no nontrivial cycles' open.
why_not_done_yet: 'No cycles for all k' is the 9x+1 analogue of the Collatz nontrivial-cycle problem. Baker-type bounds control cycles with a bounded number of local minima, but not cycles with arbitrarily many. Route (ii) is the qx+1 divergence problem, and no qx+1 orbit with q>=5 has ever been proved divergent. The sweep's exact enumeration (k<=1000; k<=3000 unrefereed) cannot reach all k. Positive drift (log(9/4) per odd step) makes divergence heuristically certain, but nothing turns that heuristic into a proof for even one orbit.
smallest_publishable_step: 9n+1 has no cycle with at most m local minima, for every k. The m=1 (circuit) case is essentially immediate. A circuit start is n = (9^k - 2^k)/(7(2^K - 9^k)), and n must be congruent mod 2^k to the 2-adic fixed point -1/7, so n >= c*2^k. A Rhin/LMN lower bound for |K log 2 - k log 9| gives n <= poly(k), so circuits are impossible beyond a small k, and a check showed none for k < 400. Extending to m <= ~50-70 with Simons-de Weger is standard. Check the qx+1 cycle literature (Steiner-type results) for novelty first.

Another: prove this specific orbit diverges by some non-congruence (archimedean or automatic) certificate. Theorem A rules out every congruence argument at every modulus.

system: split5_1_s27 (even n/2; 1 mod 4 -> 5n+1; 3 mod 4 -> n+1). Same question as CLS-064
best_route: GLOBAL has no route. Measured drift is -0.19 per step, so this is a no-divergence and no-cycles problem of 3x+1 type. The weaker statement is very tractable: transplant the split5_3 machinery (census/round2/rewriting/split5_3_s27.md) to this map. All expanding runs are governed by the single 2-adic fixed point -1/3, since 3A(x)+1 = (5/2)(3x+1). So a run of length k forces 2^k | 3x+1 and gives the recursion K <= log(m) * ((log_2(5/2))^r - 1)/log(5/2). Combine that with a range certificate (the residue-tree checker adapts directly, say to 2^48), Matveev applied to 5^K 2^-L - 1, and two continued-fraction reductions of log_2 5. Together they give 'no new cycle with <= 100 runs'. No new idea is needed beyond adapting the scripts.
why_not_done_yet: The sweep only did the one-run case (the cycle {1,3}), and it quoted the LMN constant from memory. The multi-run split5_3 argument came from a separate, later effort and was never ported to sister maps.
smallest_publishable_step: Every positive cycle other than {1,6,3,4,2} and the 35-cycle through 13 has more than 100 expanding runs and more than 10^6 steps, together with verified convergence below 2^48 and H(X)=O(X^c), c<1, for starts that never drop below themselves. This looks like weeks of work (5 for the variant).

best_route: GLOBAL is a 3x+1 variant whose odd branch is 3n+1 on most classes. It is at least as resistant as Collatz in spirit, though it is not formally equivalent. system: yah_avoid57 (n=5,7 mod 8 -> 1; else Collatz). Question: does every orbit enter (1,4,2)? This is Yolcu-Aaronson-Heule Conjecture 4.14, a $500 prize problem.
best_route: YAH Prop. 4.15 already reduces the problem to the partial map G: A(n)=(3n+1)/4 on 1 mod 32, B(n)=(9n+7)/8 on 57 mod 64, halt otherwise. B-runs have the closed form B^r(n)+7 = (9/8)^r (n+7) and need 8^r | n+7. A contracts. The heuristic is strongly favourable: a step survives with probability 3/64, and the surviving 2-adic set is a thin Cantor set (growth rate equal to the plastic number, exponent 0.406). This is unlike plain Collatz, whose drift is near zero. The missing lemma is that no positive integer other than 1 has an infinite G-orbit. That says an integer orbit cannot stay inside a thin 2-adic Cantor set, which has the same shape as Erdos's ternary-digits-of-2^n problem. Any route has to control the 2-adic digits of n+7 after multiplication by 9^r 3^a. Counting stalls because improving the X^0.406 bound needs equidistribution of E modulo 3^k, the standard barrier. My quick check: the recursion #E(X) <= sum_w #E(X*mult_w), without the mod-3^k constraint, gives no gain, because (3/4)^s+(9/8)^s > 1 for every s. I see no route that avoids this.
why_not_done_yet: The local methods (residue graph plus potential, SAT and matrix interpretations, valuation runs) provably fail. The 2-adic point -7 is a B-fixed point with slope 9/8, and that cycle persists mod 2^j for every j. Each B-run is finite by valuation, but ruling out an infinite interleaving of expanding B-runs with contracting A-steps is exactly the 3x+1 mechanism. YAH's automated search failed, and it is a stated prize problem. Cycles are not the bottleneck: a G-cycle needs R < 2.44a (R B-steps, a A-steps) and is a Collatz cycle, so known Collatz cycle-length bounds already exclude short ones. The divergent orbit or very long cycle is the real difficulty, and the earlier agents correctly found nothing new there. I rate it 2 rather than 1 because it does not contain Collatz, its heuristic is strongly subcritical, and it is the weakest prize problem in its family.
smallest_publishable_step: A sharp threshold result, checked numerically here. (i) Every C-trajectory that does not reach 1 meets 5 mod 8, 7 mod 8 or 505 mod 512. This tightens the sweep's Prop. 3(a), which used 57 mod 64 (measure 1/64), to a single class of measure 1/512. Proof: a B-run of length >= 3 starting at n needs 8^3 | n+7, i.e. n = 505 mod 512 (verified exhaustively mod 512*64). If such runs are excluded, every G-block B^j A with j <= 2 maps x to at most (243x+421)/256 < x for x >= 33. So block starts descend into [1,32], where the only G-point is the fixed point 1. (ii) The next rung, the class -7 mod 8^4, is blocked for every local method: the word B^3 A has the 2-adic rational fixed point -5069/139 (verified A(B^3(x)) = x), with slope (9/8)^3(3/4) = 1.068 > 1. So the ladder {5,7} union {-7 mod 8^r} is provable exactly for r <= 3. This is modest, a short note or a remark, but the proof is complete and new relative to the census notes.

system: up_ct3 (n=7 mod 8 -> n+8 trap; else accelerated Collatz T). Question: is the divergent set exactly the trap basin, with (1 2) the only untrapped cycle? The sweep proved this is exactly YAH Conjecture 4.13, a $500 prize problem, and it implies CLS-056.
best_route: An untrapped orbit has a 111-free T-parity word. Contraction holds only when the window ones-density is below log2/log3 = 0.6309, and 111-free words reach 2/3. So a counterexample, divergent or a long cycle, must have long-run ones-density in the narrow band [0.631, 0.667]. Such a word is almost entirely 110-blocks: at least about 2.44 consecutive 110-blocks on average between interruptions. A 110-block acts as x -> (9x+5)/8 on 3 mod 8 (verified), so x+5 scales by 9/8 and a run of k blocks needs 8^k | x+5. The open core is therefore the CLS-056 structure centred at -5 instead of -7, with a richer set of interruptions: finite valuation runs interleaved with short contracting blocks. The missing lemma is the same digit-control statement as CLS-056, with strictly less constraint. No new idea is visible.
why_not_done_yet: It is literally a named prize conjecture, and it is stronger than CLS-056. The census proved that the window/descent method fails at every window length: the class with word (110)^j expands by (9/8)^j. It also proved that congruence arguments fail, because the 2-adic integer -5 has the untrapped T-cycle -5 -> -7 -> -10. On top of that there are infinitely many expanding 2-adic cycles (110)^k 10 for k >= 3 (density (2k+1)/(3k+2) > 0.6309), so no finite set of extra trap classes recovers a descent proof. Its odd-step density sits above the critical value, which is the regime the census ladder (up_ct58 proved, up_ct3 open) identified as the Collatz-hard side. I rate it 1 because it is the strongest of the YAH single-class prize problems and needs at least what CLS-056 needs.
smallest_publishable_step: Weaker variants are either folklore or already proved. The X^0.879 density bound is in the sweep. The 'trap set of arbitrarily small measure' ladder follows from the plain-Collatz version. Cycles with few blocks are covered by existing Collatz cycle bounds (Eliahou, Simons-de Weger, Hercher) plus Barina's 2^68. The only clean new statement I see is a structural lemma: any untrapped divergent orbit or nontrivial untrapped cycle has a parity word made of 110-runs (valuation-controlled at -5) whose interruptions have upper density at most about 1/3.44. Pair it with the CLS-056 threshold theorem as the analogous provable rung, e.g. a proof of 'meets 7 mod 8 or -5 mod 2^m' for the largest m where the descent still closes. That rung, if it exists, needs the same exit analysis as CLS-056 and has not been checked.
